President Trump's apparent belief that, as president, he can pardon himself from any wrongdoing has already been ruled out by the Constitution and the courts. But it's worth recalling why that rule exists and why we have it.
In July 1974, the House Judiciary Committee, then chaired by the late Rep. John Conyers (D-Mich.), issued a report on possible impeachment proceedings against President Richard M. Nixon. One of the first things it did was to note that a president can be indicted and tried for any crime, but that he cannot be pardoned for that crime. Later, in October 1974, the House Judiciary Committee issued a final report on impeachment, at which point the Constitution's pardon clause was examined again. It was explained that no one can pardon himself.

Since China now produces more scientific research than the United States, many people assume that the country is on the cusp of becoming an innovation powerhouse. Yet the latest data on Chinese innovation suggest that this is unlikely.
China’s research spending is indeed growing, but it’s growing more slowly than in other nations, and the growth in the number of Chinese scientists is not keeping pace with the growing number of their peers around the world.
Moreover, more Chinese researchers are getting government funding to do science than those in the United States or Europe. But China invests its government money more inefficiently, and its scientists are more likely to work in “backward and obsolete” science than scientists in other countries.
The picture gets even bleaker when you consider how much government money China is spending on the military and how China is trying to export its technology, rather than the more innovative ideas generated in its universities.
